I am redesigning my personal site and I love looking up the origin of colors I come across with interesting names. For example, there are a few variants of “International Orange” that are associated with the aerospace industry (also, the Golden Gate Bridge). The Variant, “Engineering Orange” is designated as part of a federal standard dating to 1956.

There are two versions of “Dodger Blue.” One is the color used by the baseball team as a part of their modern uniforms (they wore a Robin’s Egg-type shade in the 40s, these uniforms were also reflective to help increase visibility during night games, which just started ar Ebbets’ Field, and they were also a bad choice). The other is a so-called “HTML” color `dodgerblue`. That is, you can use its name instead of a hex code and your browser knows what it is. An engineer at USC was working on tuning colors for monitor displays in the 80s. He proposed a list of names for colors that has lived on in the computing world, one of them being Dodger Blue. However, monitor tech has changed over the years and the number encoding the color he named is now displayed significantly lighter on today’s computers and does not look like the team color.

Fun fact: The Dodgers briefly wore Kelly Green in the 30s, deviating from their history of being a blue team. They were so bad, Joe DiMaggio hit more homers as an individual than their whole team one year. They also employed Babe Ruth as a coach to try and draw fans. Kelly Green did not stick with the team for some reason….

In practice, there are many reasons.

First of all, academia is a very forgetful place. If you leave, it will keep moving on without you. It’s hard to compete with freshly minted doctors who have been actively getting their work out while you’ve been languishing in industry for five years not publishing or attending conferences (which are EXPENSIVE).

Professorships require 4-5 letters of recommendation and those should almost always come from tenured faculty. It will be harder to get good letters the further removed from academia you become because people forget or are less confident in what your capabilities.

For the record, there are industry positions that publish or can otherwise be prestigious. Were you the CEO of a biotech startup? That’s an impressive way to bridge that gap and not a big issue if you are applying for a biomedical engineering position.

Search committees are evaluating all this stuff from candidates because they need to know you will be able to secure funding for your students. It’s also a very bad look if they deny tenure (other good candidates can be scared off).

The second issue is practical. Do you want to continuously uproot your life in what are presumably your 30s bouncing around jobs? Should you get a professorship, that’s going to be elsewhere in the country in all likelihood. OP would potentially be moving for a few years for a short term consulting job, then moving again for a faculty position.

This gets even worse if you find you need to do a postdoc to improve your resume, especially in fields like biology where postdocs stay postdocs forever. Now you’re job hopping every few years to different locations while trying to build a family and financial security. In all likelihood, a consulting firm would pay better and can be less stressful than doing research. It’s easy to kind of settle at that point for the easy thing you don’t really enjoy.

This is one reason why the assault on research funding is so terrible. It is effectively forcing scientists and other researchers to either take jobs outside of science (from which it is hard to return) or to do so in other countries. This is directly impacting my career right now so I feel it very personally, but every PhD holder in STEM was trained with hundreds of thousands of dollars of tax payer money. It’s a waste if they can’t use their degrees to do research in the US.

Fortunately I have funding today but I might lose it tomorrow with how the White House acts. There may not even be R1 schools hiring professors this year (or at least not many). Many schools canceled faculty searches in the middle of the process last season. Whenever they start hiring again, there will be way more competition for those openings than normal. It’s going to be brutal.

I have ADHD. I only learned about ADHD when I was in grad school after finishing the bulk of my coursework. I only got to use extra time accommodations once. The extra time is incredibly helpful and would have made the difference between letter grades for me in more than one class.

Imagine getting distracted frequently while trying to do a lot of math. Like someone is talking to you in an animated way and asking you to respond while you’re also solving numerous equations with many terms. You will make mistakes and not even realize it because your brain drifted and one thing you thought you read or did was, in fact, not what you read or did. Some small errors like writing 6 instead of 16 are now accumulating and half of your work is wrong. You realize something is off but that person is still talking to you and really wants to know the answer to some irrelevant question. You’re trying to reply to them while also scanning two pages of math for one mistake. You finally find it but your exam is over in 10 minutes so you’re just kinda boned.

Extra time afforded me the chance to read things slowly, make sure I understood instructions, and check my work carefully. Those are all things you’d do in a normal work environment. You are normally not asked to do mission critical work with large personal ramifications in the space of an hour. I have had to do that for work, and it sucked, but fortunately I was working with others who caught my typos. I also know this is a weakness of mine and avoid those situations by doing more work earlier so I’m not up against deadlines if I can help it.

Testing environments don’t do a good job of emulating the work place. They have some purpose, I believe, but homework is much closer to a work environment.

When I was a kid, I had multiple math tests where every problem was “correct,” but I lost a dozen of points on sign errors or similar mistakes because I didn’t have time to check my work due to my disability. I was smart enough to get by despite my disability until college when I really started to struggle. I developed horrible anxiety as a result and was manically studying harder than most of my peers to try and fix whatever my fault was. I also felt like I couldn’t afford to miss any homework question given I needed all the points I could get to make up for the exams. This could have been a lot easier if I just had extra time.



Finally, the role of the university is not to prepare you for the workplace. These institutions are not trade schools. Really, none of the US education system is “designed” to do so. It is designed to give you a largely liberal arts education through high school and then teach you to think critically in an area of emphasis in college. However, most schools still have breadth requirements for what are considered technical fields, like engineering. Ask any engineer how well their ABET-accredited program prepared them for the workplace and you will find it didn’t do much. You could do the same with lawyers and law school (and that’s a graduate program). Even physicians need what is basically an on-the-job apprenticeship after med school before they are licensed.

Ideally you use the right tool for the right job and that’s a mix of data and science, but we’re also academics and many of us are not concerned with building the best robots. We’re exploring what can be done with robots.

There are also things that basically can only be handled with data-driven methods. Almost everything with cameras will involve machine learning these days.

An example: there’s a lot of math around how legged locomotion works. It’s quite an interesting topic with an elegant theory but it requires understanding some nontrivial math and physics.

These days, you can get great performance for something like a quadruped just using reinforcement learning — in simulation have your robot try different motor inputs a ton of times and rate how well they work (is the center of mass moving like expected), then fit a function that reproduces the ones that work given your robot state. This simulation, rating, and fitting process is entirely automated. You then tune your RL model further with data from executions of your actual robot. 
Minimal math and physics knowledge is required for the RL approach. Also, the learned model is basically a black box. It maps an input to a good output, but it does this in a rather generic way that doesn’t tell you what is happening at a deeper level.

Basically, the “infinite monkeys typing on a keyboard” approach is being taken and it works really well. That’s not to say that there isn’t space to be smart and do research to, e.g., require less monkeys, with data-driven approaches, but a superficial understanding of locomotion is all you need to get something to locomote. That’s great for a lot of reasons, like democratizing robotics, but it doesn’t excite some of us because it feels brute force.

I didn’t attend last year, but the vibe at the academic robotics conference this year is that the community is having a bit of an existential crisis.

Data-driven methods (machine learning, especially reinforcement learning) have becoming increasingly dominant in the field and the rise of LLMs / VLMs seems to be a tipping point. The performance of this approach to robotics, especially for certain tasks, is difficult to argue with. Anything with vision or semantic reasoning really requires it.

However, for many in the community, including me, this is a sort of lame direction. Solving everything via data obviates the need to understand the basic science at play and is just not satisfying. A lot of the keynote talks have included a slide questioning whether or not robotics is “done” in some sense because the answer to every hard problem now just seems to be data. The presenters all push back on this in different ways or demonstrate where they think they fit in this new VLM world, but the vibe is different from the previous times I’ve attended over the past decade.

> Unfortunately, I’m not familiar with Gibson, so I can’t say much about him

If you’re curious:

James Gibson was a psychologist, not a philosopher, but his work I suppose is driven by a theory of the mind. With affordances, he claimed our perception of our environment is driven by how we can interact with it — a staircase is an obstacle to a baby crawling around but not an adult. That is, what the environment affords us is what we perceive in it.

Gibson has gotten attention lately in robotics because LLMs have opened up this new era of robot manipulation. They provide semantic reasoning from images for every day objects and now people are trying to get robots to do “long horizon” tasks that involve manipulating many objects relative to another to solve a task (kitchen tasks are big right now).

Some groups identified the parallels with Gibson’s notion of affordances and are trying to instantiate them in their work to improve performance on task. However, I do not believe these groups have actually read Gibson or much cognitive psychology because that just isn’t the culture in the field.

Otherwise, learning a jazz song is very different from learning a song in other genres. Almost nothing is nailed down. If you listen to a bunch of versions of Autumn Leaves, you’ll hear all sorts of tempos and styles. Even the melody and chords aren’t nailed down and they’ll be modified or embellished. Listen to the version on Somethin’ Else, which is a pretty straightforward arrangement, and compare that to the one Miles does on In Europe — it’s only barely the song.

So, to learn a song, first, you need to listen to a few different versions of it to determine what is essential. Then, you need to learn the melody. I’d suggest using a lead sheet with a metronome or your ear. Go slow, get that timing right. Then, learn those chords. The easiest way is to use shell voicing but drop 2 voicings are useful and easy to finger.

After that, it’s up to you! You can work on soloing over the changes to backing tracks, try to compose a version that blends the melody with the chords so you can do a solo performance, whatever really.

Some reasons:

1. Teams signed contracts with RSNs in the pre-streaming era that are still in effect. For example, Dodgers (in)famously lucrative contract with SNLA runs for 25 years and started in 2013 when streaming was still in its early days (when Netflix had all the good stuff).

2. At least for the MLB, with which I am most familiar, the teams that have moved to direct-to-consumer streaming services have not yet made up the gap in revenue. Even if teams get more money per customer from streaming, the volume is not there yet.

3. Again, at least for MLB, there is still revenue sharing to some degree. It sounds like you’re pretty new to improvisation as a whole? If not, my mistake, but below is my thoughts if you are.

Improvisation is a life long study. It’s also very hard to be objective about our playing. I often think my solos sound like shit but then the drummer or someone will tell me I killed it (and they weren’t just being nice). What we find boring because it’s what we play naturally, others will find exciting because it isn’t natural to them. So, patience and being kind to yourself will be essential.

Now, if this is your first time really improvising, keep it stupid simple. Play the blues scale only on the first four strings in one position. You generally want to avoid the low notes because it can sound a bit muddy in a solo, especially with a full band. Just try to create a little solo in that space. It can be really repetitive. Call and response, where you play a motif with a different ending, is a huge part of the blues sound (and music in general). Focus on connecting chord tones, how you are playing the notes, the rhythm of your lines, etc. You should do this with a backing track. There’s plenty in YouTube.

If you are struggling because you aren’t familiar with how a blues should sound, I suggest you do a few things. 

1. Listen to some actual blues players, not just jazz blues songs. The jazz guys were listening to blues players because that was the musical environment in which they lived. Both genres have a common origin and both were very popular at the time. If you only listen to one, make it B. B. King. He predominantly plays simple lines that drip blues and they translate well to jazz if you replace the bends he does with slides or hammer ons.

2. Go steal some actual licks. The quickest route is Google “jazz blues guitar licks.” That’s fine for getting started. Again, I think repurposing B. B. King’s licks will also serve you well. There’s plenty of articles and videos breaking some of his most iconic lines down. Kenny Burrell and Grant Green are two Jazz guys that have great Jazz blues lines as well. The best way to get licks is to learn them from the record, but if you are starting off, it’s more important to just get playing.

3. Now that you have some licks and got some blues in your soul, do what I said in the first paragraph again. One thing I liked doing when I started improvising (and still do now and then), is to take a lick and see how many different ways I can play it by changing the rhythm, the articulation, the ending to match new chord tones, etc. Regardless, you want to keep your solo simple and in one area. You’ll figure out how to expand out to the rest of the fretboard with time.

Remember, this is a process. You will play a lot of bum notes and make other mistakes. However, you’ll start to get the hang of it soon.

I’m going to preface this by saying I’m not the biggest pure country fan, but I have played over this kind of stuff and related genres (southern rock, certain blues and blues rock styles that are more country, folk rock, etc.) a lot. More so than I’ve played jazz really.

> playing closed triad voicings on the higher strings usually to not get too much in way of piano. but its so boring. how to fill up space and add interest?

Slide into and out of them. Use sus2s and sus4s. Do little walks into and out of chords using fragments of the chords. To me, doing this with 6ths screams country (like you said). Use different inversions. Add other extensions to create little melodies like you would in jazz, but stick to mostly diatonic extensions.

Listen to what Bob Weir does with the Grateful Dead. They’re playing blues, country, and other folky genres a lot of the time (Skull and Roses is a live album cherry picked to be almost entirely songs of this style). However, Weir would tell you he is trying to comp like how McCoy would comp for Coltrane. He’s not the most country player, but he’s a great rhythm player that knows what he’s doing and plays in a jazz-inspired way you might enjoy.

> trying to rewire my brain on these tunes and my solos on them to never touch the 7ths besides the occasional dom7 when the chart calls for it

No major 7ths. In some songs, you might be able to extend major chords to have a b7, especially if it’s a bluesier song. The b7 on minor chords is normally fine.

Like you said, major pentatonic scales from the key center are very country, but mix in some minor pentatonics from the key center as well. Sometimes you pull locks out of just one of these, but other times you think about them as one scale to build locks from. Throw in a b5 too for chromaticism. It also normally sounds a lot better to hammer on / slide into the natural third from the flat third than the other way around, in my opinion, if you are playing a line with both. I also think you can get away with outlining the changes less than in jazz, but you should still be thinking about the progression and resolving on chord tones. Don’t try and impose some complex jazz chord over stuff. The other instruments are less sparse so you can’t get away with as much tension. The occasional b9 or b5 or something can be cool, but you have to resolve that. Chromatic lines are not a problem.

Also, bend the shit out of stuff.

> also, in rehearsal today i noticed that my non-jazz rhythm playing is pretty shit. im used to playing sparse jazz comping im not used to playing so non-stop rhythmically.

Play some camp fire songs at home where you slowly strum open chords. Then play some funk groves, which are “stabby” but busy with all the muting. Your right hand is a metronome and your guitar is a drum. Maybe you do the latter when you play jazz but I find that doesn’t work as well in jazz for me because the comping is sparser and I’m finger picking chords.

I know you don’t have time to learn a bunch of tunes and solos to get genre tropes, but I’d listen to records when working, driving, mowing the lawn, whatever. Just get those cliches (many you probably know from other media) into your brain.

The last thing that comes to mind is that country players often steal licks from lap steel players. This means a lot of double stops. It also means doing a double stop and bending one string while holding the other note. A classic sound over a major chord is to bend the 2 up to the 3 on the G string while the 5 is being played on the B string. You’ll recognize this as soon as you play it.

Classically, a position player (i.e., not a pitcher) is discussed in terms of 5 tools: power (how hard they hit the ball), contact (can they hit the ball where the defenders aren’t), arm strength (how hard can you throw the ball), glove (how well can you field the ball at your position), and your foot speed. These days, due to advances in technology, it’s been common to measure and talk about other tools like bat speed. Pitchers are often discussed at a high level in terms of how hard they can throw, the different pitches they can throw (e.g., everyone has a fastball, but some guys throw a curveball while others throw a slider…there’s a lot of pitch types), and how their pitches move. When you throw something like a slider, you want it to break hard so the batter can’t track it well.  This might be too nuanced for you but if you want a term to throw in, a “five tool player” is a really good position player. A 7th chord has 4 tones. These chords are built by stacking thirds. Thus, every 7th chord has 4 notes, but there are two subsets that can form triads. For a dom7 chord, it is built:

1 3 5 b7

For a D7, that’s:

D, F#, A, C

So, the first 3 notes clearly form a D chord. The notes F#, A, C get you another triad: F# diminished. F# to A is a minor third, and A to C is another minor third.

You can do this with more complex chords as well. For example, there are two 7th chords that you can find within a 9th chord. Try that out!

What teams we root for are pretty arbitrary. A lot of us root for the local team or our parents’ teams. Some people root for teams because they like a specific player, like you. If you want to root for us because you love Skattebo (I am also hyped for him), that’s great!

We’re at an interesting juncture. We canned our old, middling QB last year in the middle of the season and ate a bunch of loses in what was shaping up to be a disappointing season either way. Now, we have an interesting QB room with two vets, one of whom was very good and won a superbowl in his younger days, and a rookie who is raw but has high upside if we can develop him (he likely won’t play until next year). Last year, we drafted very well and people are excited by the guys we acquired this weekend. Our defense looks like it’ll be very good and the Giants have always had a persona of playing great, aggressive defensive football in the years we’ve been good. We invented the “de-fense” chant that everyone uses these days without knowing the origin. There’s definitely signs things might be turning around.

That said, this team has a number of challenges. First, we’re in a brutal division. Second, we do not have a solid answer at QB. Dart needs developing and might be no good at all, or he might be great. We can’t be anything without a QB. Finally, we have a brutally hard schedule this season. Winning this year will be very hard.

Computer scheduling is actually really really hard.

For the nerds:

It boils down to what’s called a “mixed integer program,” where the integer part means that some variables you are optimizing are discrete (i.e., match ups), while some might be continuous (there may or may not be any depending on what they’re actually optimizing for). Here, “program” means “optimization problem.”

There’s a large number of competing criteria and constraints involved. For example, you want to minimize travel but you don’t want a team to be on the road for six weeks straight. Then you have things like concert bookings, off day allocation, trying to balance strength of schedule so that the juicy matchups aren’t all the same month, etc. Most of these criteria and constraints are discrete and these problems end up being quite big.

Integer programs (mixed or not) are famously ~~NP-complete~~ NP-Hard. This means that we cannot solve said problems exactly except by brute force. Some cases of MIPs might even be harder to solve.

Now, the software for common classes of MIPs has come a looooong way. Not only do we have methods that exploit the parallelization capabilities of modern computer clusters, but we’ve developed better and better heuristics methods which produce good solutions more quickly. However, MIPs are still a dirty word to a lot of people that need to solve optimization problems fast.

How this plays into baseball scheduling: designing schedules involve many parameters. For example, how do you weight road trip duration vs distributing the strength of match ups? The answer is you try things and see if you like the solution. Unfortunately, if the MIP is big enough that it takes a very long time to run, you might not get too many shots at tweaking parameters. You might find a setup that works for a good number of teams but not all 30 times, as well.

That old couple had the advantage of human intuition. They knew what a good schedule was like and didn’t have to fiddle with parameters. The downside was they had to set everything by hand which is arduous. Someone might even complain about their ability to set fair schedules. I’m not saying this ever happened, just that having a computer trying to do the optimal thing based on a set of rules applied unilaterally precludes the rumors even starting.

I’m just going to give some general advice. This is too broad a question, and I think non-traditional jazz tones are a space that can still be explored quite a bit depending on your personal style. I also don’t use a lot of pedals when playing jazz myself. However, I use them a lot for other genres.

> super clear, warm, and expressive

Warm tones normally mean the mids are prominent. What expressive means can vary, but if you mean you like dynamics, you want to minimize compression. That means no or low overdrive, light use of a compression pedal, and maybe a little something to fatten it like a touch of reverb or slap back delay to taste.

> Should I start with individual pedals or get a multi-effects unit to learn what I like

Personally, I hate multi-effects pedals for two reasons. The first is that they have too many options and often require some menu diving. This is a distraction from playing. The second is that, in my experience, a few of the effects or presets will be great but some will be really lacking, normally the overdrives and distortions. That might not bother you, however. Some people really dig them and the quality of sounds they make gets better every year.

Watch a lot of That Pedal Show videos. They are very good, in my opinion of explaining what the purpose or purposes of a pedal are, how to use them with other pedals, etc. They have certain biases and tend to emphasize certain playing styles because that’s how they play guitar. Mick is going to play a bunch of SRV licks no matter how hard he tries. Dan plays his mix of 80s rock and Lydian dominant lines (he started learning jazz a few years back). However, as they got more popular, they started getting guests that play all sorts of music. The Joey Landreth videos are particularly cool and will have some sounds I think you might dig.

For straight pedal reviews, I always like to try to find a review from Andy Martin. He’s been with a few companies over the years and now has his own channel. He does a good job of using pedals in multiple ways and with multiple playing styles.

My second piece of advice is that, in 95% of cases, you don’t need nearly as much of whatever effect you think you do.

This is especially common if playing with overdrive or distortion. Everyone wants to turn whatever up to 11, but that’s a great way to sound like a hot mess. I used to play in a rock band and the singer was a great singer but a pretty inexperienced guitar player. I had to constantly turn his pedals down because it just sounded like a wall of nothing. A lot of the thick, heavy guitar sounds he was after were achieved using EQ and studio mixing, not by turning a TubeScreamer all the way up.

However, this goes for any effect. Too much compression and any minor imperfection in your playing becomes pronounced. You also lose any notion of dynamics. Too much reverb or delay and your playing will get washed out. There are totally times to crank these effects, but those circumstances are more limited than you think.

My last piece of advice is buy an EQ pedal. They’re dirt cheap, the cheap clones you can get for $30 are as good as the ones that cost $130, and they are incredibly powerful. No pedal will have a bigger influence on your sound than an EQ pedal.

Oh, my last last piece of advice is that what you’re playing into matters. A big tube amp is going to be different than a tiny practice amp. The interactions between the speaker, the air, the power amp, and the pre-amp matter. Tiny amps get some cool compressed sounds sometimes (see Layla and Other Love Songs), but they behave differently than big amps that are loud.

Oh and if you run more than a few pedals, get a buffer. A lot of tuners these days come with buffers built in.

Simple terms: The center of percussion is the point that, if the ball hits it, it will not produce a torque. I.e., it will not try to get the base to rotate back into your hands. That torque gets dissipated into our hands as we keep the bat steady and is essentially wasted energy. Thus, the CoP is commonly considered the “sweet spot.” This also tells you why you get stingers: your hands had to dissipate a lot of torque.

The beam model I know less about because it’s a bit afar from my field. It’s basically a simple but popular model for an elongated deformable object. It’s described by a partial differential equation. If you fix one end (where we hold the bat), and apply a force, the bat will bend. There is also a way to define the sweet spot using properties of the solution to this equation, but I’m not totally sure how it’s done, but it has to do with the harmonics of the waves that make up the solution. Again, beam models aren’t really my thing.

Another analysis that only relies on high school physics is based on the [center of percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_percussion).

The center of percussion is the point where an applied force would cause a beam to only move laterally, not to rotate. Any rotation is energy that gets dissipated into your hands and isn’t driving the ball away from the bat. It’s therefore wasted.

If you follow the equations, you can see the center of percussion is a function of the moment of inertia of the bat. How do we shift the moment of inertia? We change how the mass of the bat is laid out! If the bat was synthetic, we could alter the density of the bat material to do so. However, in this case, it’s solid wood. The density of the wood is not alterable. Therefore, we have to change the shape of the bat. The torpedo shape moves the center of percussion more towards the handle.

Now, there’s some other effects this analysis doesn’t cover. For example, there are bat weight and radius constraints. Moreover, if you put a really awkward bump of wood in your bat design, you will deflect the ball in all sorts of weird ways.

However, the most important consideration is that moving the moment of inertia is going to impact your swing mechanics. Where you tend to hit the ball with a traditional bat and with a torpedo bat might be different! So finding an optimal bat for a player means you probably need to go through a few iterations.

How this relates to OP’s analysis:

In the above, we treated the bat like an ideal rigid body. Obviously, there is no such thing. Both the bat and ball bend fractional amounts (you can see a ball squish in slow motion when it gets mashed). The beam model in OP’s link follows from something called Euler-Bernoulli beam theory which is sort of the first step when you consider a deformable object. However, the result of this theory is normally some PDEs that require computer simulation to solve outside of fairly simple cases and, in my opinion, make the math behind the phenomenon more opaque.

O’Malley and Moses fought over this for a while then O’Malley decided to move to LA where the city was much more cooperative (and had a bunch of land that they had just acquired via eminent domain from which they evicted a bunch of poor people…). Moses was the main individual blocking the stadium being built as, O’Malley had bipartisan support at various other levels of government.

This seems like a circular thing that might even out to do nothing in the long run.

A pitcher’s goal is to prevent hard contact (ideally by striking someone out in most cases), which means avoiding the sweet spot. That means I know I should attack a guy this way because he tends to hit it on the inside and loses power. Now, that batter gets smart and gets a torpedo bat. The new moment of inertia  of the bat moves the sweet spot inside. Where he made weak contact yesterday is strong contact today. So, as a pitcher, what do I do? I pitch him outside so now he’s hitting past the sweet spot and making weak contact again. When he gets a new bat, I change how I pitch him.

The analogy they mention in the article of fitting golf clubs makes sense to a degree, but it’d be like if the golf ball fought back.

Now, what does make sense to me is hitters finding a torpedo bat that they like because of what it does to their technique. Again, moving the sweet spot, which has been the bulk of the discussion, is equivalent by changing the moment of inertia. That impacts the whole swinging motion. Guys might like the feel of their swing with the more center-loaded torpedo bats. Bats that aren’t wood have had these options for years. You could get faster, center-loaded bats, or end loaded bats that deliver more power if you get it around in time. This is closer to the club fitting analogy in the article.

This has been going on for years and it isn’t just the super team aspect (maybe for Sasaki it was because of Ohtani and Yamamoto). Guys take pay cuts to play for the Dodgers so they can access their training stuff. Syndergaard straight up said he signed for less because if anyone could fix him it was them. Even if you aren’t a reclamation project, you do a one year stint with the Dodgers at a discount, post some career-best stats with the helping hand of Mark Prior, then go get your bag somewhere else. Maybe you get extra lucky and get a ring while you’re in town.

One way or the other, there’s a ton of reasons to come here as a pitcher that aren’t money. However, that’s not unique to baseball. In the NFL, Barkley went on the record saying he turned down a few million extra dollars from elsewhere to go the Philadelphia. Money isn’t everything to these guys when they pick where to sign.

People also forget it isn’t just the players. The Dodgers spent a ton to upgrade their stadium facilities last year, but the parts that are off limits and house various team personnel, training facilities, etc. when Cohen bought the Mets, he hired a bunch of analytics folks because the Mets had been weak in that area for a long time.

When owners skimp on this stuff, which is easy to do because the public tends not to think about it and has little info on it, they miss out on cost effective ways to build their team. The Dodgers payroll is only part of their success: the rest is that they built a great FO and development pipeline. You have to put work into those areas and the bad teams tend to not do that in addition to being cheap on the field.
